metadata.title: Bayes' Theorem: The Positive That's Usually Wrong
metadata.audience: a curious adult who has seen 'the test is 99% accurate' and wants to know what a positive means

beats.narration_text: Hello, this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: a test that catches ninety-nine percent of cases says I'm positive. How likely is it that I'm actually sick? Show me with real numbers.

show.event: composer card fades in on cream
greeting 'Hello, Liam' types above the composer
the ask types in
runningText 'working through the math…' appears
three result lines cascade in

props.segment: Bayes' Theorem: The Positive That's Usually Wrong
props.command: A test that catches 99% of cases says I'm positive. How likely is it that I'm actually sick? Show me with real numbers.
output: sensitivity: the test catches 99 of every 100 sick people
base rate: only 1 in 100 people have the disease

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask lands answered; Liam introduced in first breath.

beats.narration_text: A positive test can still be a false alarm. When a disease is rare, false alarms from the healthy outnumber the real cases. What decides it is the base rate: how common the disease is.

show.event: cream page holds; caret blinks
types "A positive test\nmeans you're probably sick."
'means you're probably sick' turns terracotta, hesitates, backspaces
types 'can still be a false alarm'
final lines settle

props.text:
A positive test
means you're probably sick.
props.replacementWords: can still be a false alarm

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — misconception corrected: a positive is not 99% sure; with a rare disease most positives are false alarms.

learn.question: A test that catches 99% of cases says positive. How likely am I to be sick?
learn.action: One square, 'you', on the stage; the test chip runs over it; the result stamps POSITIVE.
learn.observation: The only numbers on screen are the 99% and the positive.
learn.inference: Everyone's first answer is 99%; nothing on screen yet can check it.
learn.next_question: What happens if we run this test on a whole crowd, not one person?

beats.narration_text: You take a test for a rare disease. It catches ninety-nine percent of the people who have it. Your result: positive. So how worried should you be? Hold on to your first answer. We're going to count.

show.event: one ink square 'you' draws on, centre stage
test chip 'catches 99% of cases' slides across the square
result stamp 'positive' lands beside the square — the beat's terracotta
MathTex P(sick) = \, ? writes beside it, the '?' large
the square and stamp shrink toward the top-left corner (the grid's first cell)

shot.visual_intent: One ink square ('you') with a terracotta POSITIVE stamp and an unanswered P(sick) = ?. The square is the persistent object the PAYOFF brings back.
shot.motion_claim: The stamp landing is the event; the closing shrink hands the square to the grid in B11 (state factory).

learn.question: What does the test do across a whole crowd?
learn.action: Count up 10,000 squares; mark the 100 sick (a 10 × 10 block, top left); run the test on them.
learn.observation: 99 of the 100 sick stay lit; 1 fades (missed).
learn.inference: Among the sick, the 99% does exactly what it promised.
learn.next_question: And what does the same test do to everyone who is healthy?

beats.narration_text: Make it people. Ten thousand of them, one square each. One percent have the disease: one hundred squares. Run the test on them. It catches ninety-nine. One slips through. So far, the ninety-nine percent is doing exactly what it promised.

show.event: 125 × 80 isotype grid (pitch 0.068 u, 8.5 × 5.44 u, left of a counter column; IsotypeGrid pattern from explainer/manim/animated_graphics.py) counts up in reading order, dim; 'you' sits in it as an outline ring
a 10 × 10 block of 100 cells, top left, turns ink on 'one hundred squares'; label 'sick: 100'
a scan bar sweeps the sick cells on 'Run the test'
99 stay ink, counter 'positive: 99'
1 square fades to ghost — terracotta ring on it for the sentence 'One slips through'

shot.visual_intent: Isotype grid of 10,000 squares (125 per row, pitch 0.068 u); the sick a 10 × 10 block (top left) in ink, healthy dim, missed/cleared fade to ghost. Counters in EB Garamond from evidence.json.
shot.motion_claim: The grid filling, then the scan bar filtering the sick block, is the instance: sensitivity shown as a count.

learn.question: What does the same test do to the 9,900 healthy people?
learn.action: Sweep the scan bar over the remaining healthy cells; 95% fade (cleared), 5% stay lit.
learn.observation: 495 healthy squares stay lit — five times as many as the sick who tested positive.
learn.inference: A small false-alarm rate times a huge healthy crowd is a big number.
learn.next_question: So — what's the chance for someone who tested positive?

beats.narration_text: Now the other nine thousand nine hundred, the healthy ones. The test clears ninety-five percent of them. But five percent light up anyway. Five percent of nine thousand nine hundred is four hundred ninety-five false alarms. Five times as many as the sick people it caught.

show.event: scan bar returns to row 2 and sweeps down the remaining healthy cells
9,405 cleared squares fade to ghost as the bar passes
495 squares stay lit, scattered — they flash terracotta on 'light up anyway'
counter 'false alarms: 495' beside 'positive: 99'
the 495 settle to dim; two counters held side by side

shot.visual_intent: Same grid, same objects; the 495 false positives are seeded positions (seed in scenes.py) and stay lit dim after their terracotta flash.
shot.motion_claim: Second instance, same parameter (the test), different group: false-positive rate shown as a count.

learn.question: Isn't the answer just the 99% on the box?
learn.action: Box the sick block; write 99/100; then point at the 495 lit squares outside the box.
learn.observation: The 99/100 is true — but its denominator is the sick, a crowd you don't know you're in.
learn.inference: The 99% answers a question about the sick; yours is about the positives.
learn.next_question: What if we counted inside the crowd you actually know you're in?

beats.narration_text: The natural answer is ninety-nine percent. It's the number on the box. And it's true, for this block: ninety-nine of the one hundred who are sick tested positive. But that fraction is about people already known to be sick. All you know is that you tested positive.

show.event: rectangle draws round the sick block; label 'out of the sick'
MathTex \frac{99}{100} writes beside the box
the 495 lit squares outside the box pulse once — terracotta
dim caption: 'but you only know you're positive'

shot.visual_intent: The box and its fraction are correct; the pulse of the lit squares outside it shows what the box leaves out.
shot.motion_claim: The natural attempt walked to its limit: the box is right and the wrong crowd.

learn.question: What if we counted only the crowd you're in — the positives?
learn.action: Fade every negative; the 594 positives fly together into one block (27 × 22), sick first.
learn.observation: One block: 99 ink squares, 495 dim. 'You' is somewhere in it.
learn.inference: The representation: keep only the people who match what you know.
learn.next_question: Of these, what share are sick?

beats.narration_text: So change the crowd. Keep everyone who tested positive, and let everyone else go. Here they are: ninety-nine who are sick, four hundred ninety-five who aren't. Before we count, commit to a guess. Of these lit squares, what share are sick?

show.event: all ghost (negative) squares fade out
the 594 positives fly into one 27 × 22 block, larger squares, sick first
'you' ring lands on the block's edge: you're one of these
HOLD ≥ 3 s — nothing moves on 'commit to a guess'

shot.visual_intent: The positives-only block (natural-frequency representation, Gigerenzer & Hoffrage 1995). Mark the simplification once: dim caption 'each square = one person; expected counts'.
shot.motion_claim: The re-grouping IS the reframe: the denominator changes on screen. The hold is the predict beat.

learn.question: Of the positives, what share are sick?
learn.action: The 99 ink squares stack above a fraction bar, all 594 below it; the stacks morph into numerals 99/594, which reduce to 1/6.
learn.observation: One positive in six is sick; five in six are false alarms.
learn.inference: The answer to 'how worried?' is about 17%, not 99%.
learn.next_question: Can we write that without counting squares?

beats.narration_text: Ninety-nine have the disease. Five hundred ninety-four in all. Watch the fraction shrink. One in six. Five out of six positives are healthy.

show.event: the 99 ink squares slide up and stack above a growing fraction bar
all 594 squares stream under the bar
the stacks morph into MathTex \frac{99}{594}
the fraction transforms to \frac{1}{6} — the terracotta lands on it
dim chip '≈ 16.67%' under it; held

shot.visual_intent: One continuous morph: squares become the numerator and denominator, the fraction reduces. Every object persists from B14.
shot.motion_claim: The aha is the morph itself; narration is short sentences so run_time fills the audio.

learn.question: Can we say that in general, without squares?
learn.action: Divide each count by 10,000: 99 becomes 0.99 × 0.01, then P(+|D)P(D); 594 becomes P(+); assemble P(D|+); swap D, + for A, B.
learn.observation: The equation is the fraction we just watched, written in chances.
learn.inference: Bayes' theorem: flip a conditional chance by weighing in how common each side is.
learn.next_question: What does each symbol in that line mean?

beats.narration_text: This thing deserves a name. Divide every count by ten thousand and the counts become chances. Ninety-nine becomes the sensitivity times the base rate. Five hundred ninety-four becomes the chance of any positive. What's left is Bayes' theorem. It flips a conditional chance by weighing in how common each side is.

show.event: the \frac{99}{594} from B15 slides left; '÷ 10,000' writes under each number
99 → \frac{99}{10\,000} → 0.99 \times 0.01 → P(+\mid D)\,P(D) (MathTex, staged)
594 → P(+) (MathTex)
assembles P(D\mid +) = \frac{P(+\mid D)\,P(D)}{P(+)}
D, + morph to A, B: P(A\mid B) = \frac{P(B\mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}; serif label 'Bayes' theorem' — terracotta

shot.visual_intent: The counts transform into the notation (objects → symbols, never the other way). Every equation in MathTex.
shot.motion_claim: The abstraction arrives as an endpoint: the fraction the viewer watched becomes Bayes' theorem.

learn.question: What does each symbol mean?
learn.action: Equation persists left; right band writes the two sides as sentences, the '=' as a claim, a glossary, one worked value, and the values claim (the bar has a direction).
learn.observation: Every symbol maps back to a crowd on the grid.
learn.inference: The notation is a description of the counting.

beats.narration_text: Read it piece by piece. On the left: the chance of disease, given a positive. On the right: the chance of a positive, given disease, the ninety-nine percent, times the base rate, one percent, divided by the share of everyone who tests positive. Zero point nine nine times zero point zero one, over zero point zero five nine four. One sixth. The bar has a direction. Swap its sides, and you get a different number.

show.event: LHS P(A|B) boxed (box spotlight, not underline); sentence 'chance of A once you know B'
P(B|A) boxed; glossary row 'P(B|A) · sensitivity · 0.99'
P(A) boxed; row 'P(A) · base rate · 0.01'
P(B) boxed; row 'P(B) · all positives · 0.0594'
worked value: 0.99 × 0.01 / 0.0594 = 1/6 (MathTex)
values claim: P(B|A) ≠ P(A|B) — the '≠' gets the box spotlight, terracotta

shot.visual_intent: Split stage, five zones (EQUATIONS.md / animated_graphics.EquationTangent): symbolic form persists MAIN; sentences, glossary (A = disease, B = a positive test), worked example and values claim write into SIDE.
shot.motion_claim: One moving box spotlight across equation, sentence and glossary row; ~30–40 s, explains never derives.

learn.question: So — how worried should you be?
learn.action: The HOOK's 'you' square with its positive stamp returns into the 594 block; the 1/6 sits beside it.
learn.observation: You moved from 1 in 100 to 1 in 6 — a real jump, nowhere near 99%.
learn.inference: Healthy people outnumber the sick 99 to 1, so a 5% false-alarm rate makes a crowd.
learn.next_question: How much did the base rate decide that?

beats.narration_text: Back to you. You are one of these five hundred ninety-four; one in six is sick. A positive moved you from one in a hundred to one in six: a real jump, nowhere near ninety-nine percent. The sick are outnumbered ninety-nine to one, so a small false-alarm rate makes a crowd.

show.event: the B10 'you' square + stamp return (same objects) and settle into the 594 block
MathTex \frac{1}{100} → \frac{1}{6} arrow beside the square
the 99:1 ratio: sick row vs the healthy mass flash once, terracotta on the healthy side
held: you, the block, 1/6

shot.visual_intent: The HOOK's persistent object resolved: the 'you' square inside the positives, its P(sick) = ? now 1/6.
shot.motion_claim: PAYOFF returns the HOOK object, not a redraw; the explanation check (why?) is answered on the 99:1 flash.

learn.question: How much did the base rate decide that?
learn.action: Plot P(D|+) against base rate (log axis); a ValueTracker slides the 1/6 marker along the curve.
learn.inference: The test didn't change; the crowd did. Not taught here: what a second positive does.

beats.narration_text: One number did most of that work: the base rate. Same test, rarer disease, one in a thousand: a positive means about two percent. One in ten: about sixty-nine percent. One in two: ninety-five. What this film didn't do is test you twice. That's your turn.

show.event: the 1/6 slides onto axes: base rate (log) vs chance sick given positive
marker slides left to 0.1%: reads 1.94%
slides right through 1% (1/6) to 10%: 68.75%
to 50%: 95.19%; the full curve traced in ink, marker terracotta
dim captions: 'same test: 99% sensitive, 95% specific' · 'not taught here: a second positive'

shot.visual_intent: Curve from evidence.json base_rate_curve (61 log-spaced points); labelled points 0.1% → 1.94%; 1% → 16.67%; 10% → 68.75%; 50% → 95.19%.
shot.motion_claim: The ValueTracker sweep makes the dependence a motion; the boundary is one dim line that hands off to BHTF.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The ninety-nine percent is about the sick: ninety-nine of every hundred sick people test positive. Your question is about the positives, and only ninety-nine of five hundred ninety-four are sick: one in six. The healthy outnumber the sick ninety-nine to one, so five percent false alarms make a crowd. Bayes' theorem flips the question by weighing in the base rate.

show.event: artifact page opens
four verdict lines land in narration order

props.artifactHeading: Bayes' Theorem: The Positive That's Usually Wrong
artifactLines: The 99% is about the sick: 99 of 100 sick people test positive.
Your question is about the positives: only 99 of 594 are sick, one in six.
The healthy outnumber the sick 99 to 1, so 5% false alarms make a crowd.
Bayes' theorem flips the question by weighing in the base rate.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: A test catches ninety-nine percent of people who have a disease and wrongly flags five percent of healthy people. One person in a hundred has the disease. Someone tests positive, then takes the same test again and tests positive a second time. Before calculating, guess the chance they are sick. Then count it out for a million people, show the counts after each test, and say what you had to assume about the two tests. Here's what to check. After one positive: one in six. After two: about four in five, because the first answer became the new base rate. And it should say the two results were assumed independent. A real repeat test often isn't.

show.event: composer opens — 'Your turn.'
the prompt types in full
runningText 'paste this into Claude…'
three check lines land as each is spoken
